newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Production, exports growth Serbia's top goals in H2.
newsitem.headline: Production, exports growth Serbia's top goals in H2.

text.p: Serbia's economic priorities for the second half of this year should be to boost production and exports, providing a basis to launch reforms, Belgrade businessmen said on Friday.

"We must increase production at least by 10 percent on last year. A two digit figure is like a psychological barrier regardless of the low base we started from," Milosav Filipovic, president of MINEL Holding Corporation told Reuters.
He said production increases should help to push up exports. "Rehabilitation of production capacities is the best way to start reforms," he added.

Industrial output rose 8.1 percent in January-June, compared with the same months in 1996. Exports were up 27.2 percent and imports 23.4 percent in the first half of the year compared to the same period a year ago.
Filipovic, also a member of Serbia's Chamber of Commerce managing board, said price and currency stability must remain the main prerequisites for all other economic targets.

Serbia has set very ambitious goals for its battered economy in 1997 -- currency and price stability, rises of 14 percent in production and 37 percent in exports, a higher standard of living, privatisation and reforms.
Businessmen said lack of working capital in the first half of the year meant that they failed to reach set targets and limited the revival of the economy.
"But money is here now and (cash shortages) cannot be used as an excuse for non-productivity," Filipovic said.

Filipovic reffered to 1.568 billion German marks ($874.5 million) raised through the sale of a 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija to OTE of Greece and Stet of Italy, 80 percent of which was paid immediately. The rest will be paid in January 1998.
The Serbian Development Fund, the sole recipient of the money, said it would finance exports aimed at helping cash-strapped industry revive production and double sales abroad this year.
"What we need are good export deals, but it seems there is more money available than profitable programmes," said Zika Stevic, of the Chamber's foreign economic relations board.

The Fund has already allocated the first 45 credits worth 126 million marks. The credits, with four percent interest a year, were granted for already concluded export deals. They mature in a three- to six-month period depending on the production cycle and are repayable in hard currency.
Stevic said that some of the 45 companies had received government financial support before but had never paid back.
"We have to be realistic. Some firms on the list will not be able to meet their liabilities in time," he said.

The government expects the loans to secure exports worth 656 million marks. The deals are to raise the utilisation of capacity from 55 to 80 percent and provide work for some 12,000 workers now on compulsory leave.

Jadranka Vale, head of Serbia's Centre for Development, said such a financial injection meant a lot and should be used in the most efficient way to kick-start production. It should be invested in economically viable projects, he said.
But he said the funds could not reslove all the problems facing the economy. "More money will be needed in the next stage of our development."
-- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254 ($ = 1.793 German Marks)
